subject: chemistry_2
question_text: CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue in colour whereas anhydrous CuSO₄ is colourless. Why?

mark_split.label: Water is a ligand and splits the d orbitals
No water, so no d-d transition in the visible range

verification.note: Unit 11 (d and f Block Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 8 ("8. d & f BLOCK ELEMENTS"), book pp.91-94, which prints this question on book p.91 as VSAQ 3. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK STATEMENT SHARPENED (book p.91, VSAQ 3): the printed answer says that in anhydrous CuSO₄ "due to the absence of water, crystal field splitting is not possible". Strictly that is not so — the sulphate oxygen atoms still surround Cu²⁺ and still split the d orbitals — but they produce a much weaker field than water, so the gap Δo is small and the absorption falls outside the visible range. The card writes the honest version: the splitting is too small to absorb visible light, so the solid is white. TREND AND EXCEPTION: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ and coloured in both hydrated and complexed forms; the exceptions in the series are Sc³⁺ (3d⁰) and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰), which are colourless whatever the ligand, and those are named on the sibling colour cards.

d and f Block Elements — 2 marks

steps.label: The hydrated salt is blue
lines: In CuSO₄·5H₂O the water molecules act as
They split the five d orbitals into a
lower t2g set and a higher eg set.
Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, so the eg set has one
vacancy. An electron from the lower t2g
set moves up into it: a d-d transition.
The salt absorbs orange-red light and
transmits blue, so it looks blue.
steps.why: Colour in a d-block salt needs two things at the same time: a partly filled d subshell and a set of ligands to split it. Water supplies the second. Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, so one electron can be promoted across the gap, and the energy needed for that promotion is taken from the orange-red part of white light, so the light that passes through is blue. An ion with an empty or a full d subshell, such as Sc³⁺ (3d⁰) or Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰), stays colourless whatever the ligand.
common_mistakes: Saying the blue colour comes from the sulphate ion. SO₄²⁻ has no partly filled d subshell and is colourless.
Saying Cu²⁺ is coloured on its own. Without ligands the five d orbitals are degenerate, so there is no gap to absorb across.
steps.memory_tip: Colour needs both: a partly filled d subshell and ligands to split it. Water is the ligand here.
steps.margin_note: The terms crystal field splitting and d-d transition are the marked terms. Write them in that order.

steps.label: The anhydrous salt is white
lines: In anhydrous CuSO₄ the water is gone.
Cu²⁺, and they give a much weaker field.

lines.text: Δo is too small to absorb

lines: visible light, so no d-d transition takes
Nothing visible is absorbed, so the solid
steps.why: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ in both solids, so the number of d electrons is not what changes. What changes is the ligand. Water is a stronger-field ligand than sulphate oxygen, so it gives a larger gap Δo; the smaller gap in the anhydrous salt corresponds to infrared rather than visible light, nothing in the visible range is removed, and all of it is returned, which is what a white solid is. Putting water back gives the larger gap again and the blue returns.
common_mistakes: Writing that anhydrous CuSO₄ has no d electrons. Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ in both solids; only the ligand changes.
Stopping at the word colourless. The mark is for the reason — no d-d transition in the visible range — not for the observation.
steps.memory_tip: Take the water away and the gap falls below the visible range, so there is no colour.
steps.margin_note: Finish with the reverse test: add water and the blue returns. One line, and it shows the cause.

insider_note: This is a two-part comparison, so answer it in two halves. The second half carries a full mark, and it is regularly lost by explaining the blue salt in full and then writing only "no water, so colourless" — that mark is for the reason, not for the observation.
